## Design and notation

A trial is stratified into $J \ge 2$ strata, for example by centre or by a baseline factor, and stratum $j$ has $N_{1j}$ patients in group 1 and $N_{2j}$ in group 2, both fixed by the design. Let $x_{1j}$ and $x_{2j}$ be the numbers of responders of the two groups and $z_j = x_{1j} + x_{2j}$ the number of responders of the stratum. All tests of the `Strat*` functions use $S = \sum_j x_{1j}$, the number of responders of group 1 summed over the strata. Given $z = (z_1, \ldots, z_J)$, the null expectation of $S$ is $E = \sum_j N_{1j} z_j / N_j$ with $N_j = N_{1j} + N_{2j}$, and each test rejects when $S$ is at most a lower or at least an upper critical value.

The functions follow those for two independent groups: `StratRR()`, `StratPower()` and `StratSampleSize()` for the fixed design, and `StratPowerBSSR()`, `StratBSSR()`, `StratTypeIErrorBSSR()` and `StratAlphaAdjBSSR()` for blinded sample size re-estimation.

## Tests

Five tests are available. `'CMH'` is the Cochran-Mantel-Haenszel statistic $(S - E) / \sqrt{V}$ with the hypergeometric variance $V = \sum_j N_{1j} N_{2j} z_j (N_j - z_j) / \{N_j^2 (N_j - 1)\}$, and `'Cochran'` is Cochran's statistic with the binomial variance $\sum_j N_{1j} N_{2j} z_j (N_j - z_j) / N_j^3$, the statistic of Woolson et al. (1986). `'CMH-cc'` and `'Cochran-cc'` reduce $|S - E|$ by 0.5, the continuity correction of `stats::mantelhaen.test()` and of Nam (1992). `'Strat-Fisher'` is the stratified exact conditional test of Jung (2014), which refers $S$ to its distribution given $z$, the convolution of the hypergeometric distributions of the strata.

Jung (2014, Table 2) analyses the response to thymosin in three strata of patients with bronchogenic carcinoma.

```{r jung-example}
thymosin <- array(c(10, 12, 1, 1, 9, 11, 0, 1, 8, 7, 0, 3), c(2, 2, 3))
p.exact <- stats::mantelhaen.test(thymosin, alternative = 'greater', exact = TRUE)$p.value
p.mh <- stats::mantelhaen.test(thymosin, alternative = 'greater', correct = FALSE)$p.value
round(c(exact = p.exact, mh = p.mh), 4)
```

The one-sided p-values `r sprintf('%.4f', p.exact)` and `r sprintf('%.4f', p.mh)` are those of Jung (2014) for the stratified exact test and the Mantel-Haenszel test, which `'Strat-Fisher'` and `'CMH'` compute in the same way. `StratRR()` lists the critical values of a design for every vector of stratum totals.

```{r rr}
rr <- StratRR(N1 = c(10, 12), N2 = c(10, 12), alpha = 0.025, Test = 'Strat-Fisher')
print(rr, n = 6)
```

## Power and sample size

The power is the probability of the rejection region when the numbers of responders are binomial in every group and stratum. It is computed exactly for any number of strata and any response probabilities, so the odds ratio need not be common to the strata. The normal approximation to the total sample size is formula (2.8) of Woolson et al. (1986), and with a continuity correction formula (2.3) of Nam (1992). A design is described by the fractions of the strata and the allocation ratio, and the exact search runs over the total sample size within this family.

```{r sample-size}
p2 <- c(0.3, 0.5)
p1 <- p2 * 2.5 / (1 - p2 + p2 * 2.5)
ss.std <- StratSampleSize(p1, p2, frac = c(0.4, 0.6), alpha = 0.025, tar.power = 0.8,
                          Test = 'CMH', method = 'standard')
ss.cmh <- StratSampleSize(p1, p2, frac = c(0.4, 0.6), alpha = 0.025, tar.power = 0.8,
                          Test = 'CMH')
ss.exact <- StratSampleSize(p1, p2, frac = c(0.4, 0.6), alpha = 0.025, tar.power = 0.8,
                            Test = 'Strat-Fisher')
c(standard = ss.std$N, CMH = ss.cmh$N, exact = ss.exact$N)
```

With a common odds ratio of 2.5, the normal approximation gives a total of `r ss.std$N` patients, at which the exact power of the CMH test is `r sprintf('%.3f', ss.std$Power)`. The exact search gives `r ss.cmh$N` patients for the CMH test and `r ss.exact$N` for the stratified exact test, whose conditional control of the type I error rate makes it conservative.

## Blinded sample size re-estimation

At an interim analysis the numbers of responders of every stratum can be counted without unblinding. The blinded estimate of the pooled response probability of stratum $j$ is $s_j$ divided by the interim size of the stratum. It is divided between the groups with the assumed effect `Delta.A`, common to the strata on the scale `effect`, and the total sample size is re-estimated for these probabilities and divided between the strata as in the planned design. With two strata the final sizes depend on the interim data only through $(s_1, s_2)$, and the power is computed exactly by enumeration. With a common odds ratio the planning probabilities of a stratum whose pooled estimate is close to 0 or 1 are close to each other, so the examples bound the final total by twice the planned total with `N.max`.

```{r bssr}
plan <- StratSampleSize(p1, p2, frac = c(0.5, 0.5), alpha = 0.025, tar.power = 0.8,
                        Test = 'CMH', method = 'standard')
pooled <- (p1 + p2) / 2
res <- StratPowerBSSR(p = rbind(pooled, pooled + 0.1), Delta.A = 2.5, Delta.T = 2.5,
                      N1 = plan$N1, N2 = plan$N2, omega = 0.5, r = 1, alpha = 0.025,
                      tar.power = 0.8, Test = 'CMH', effect = 'OR',
                      ss.method = 'standard', N.max = 2 * plan$N)
res
```

When the pooled response probabilities are those of the planning (the first row), the power of the re-estimation design is `r sprintf('%.3f', res$power.BSSR[1])` with an expected total of `r sprintf('%.1f', res$E.N[1])`. When they are 0.1 higher in both strata, the re-estimation adjusts the sample size and the power is `r sprintf('%.3f', res$power.BSSR[2])`, while that of the fixed design is `r sprintf('%.3f', res$power.TRAD[2])`.

## Type I error rate

Under the null hypothesis both groups of stratum $j$ respond with the probability $\theta_j$. Given the interim and the second-stage numbers of responders of a stratum, the numbers of responders of group 1 are hypergeometric whatever $\theta_j$, so with two strata the type I error rate is a polynomial in $(\theta_1, \theta_2)$. `StratTypeIErrorBSSR()` computes its coefficients in the products of the Bernstein bases of the two strata, evaluates it on a grid, and certifies its largest value over the rectangle spanned by the grid: the rectangle is subdivided until the largest coefficient of every piece exceeds the largest value found by at most $10^{-12}$.

```{r tie}
tie <- StratTypeIErrorBSSR(Delta.A = 2.5, N1 = c(20, 20), N2 = c(20, 20), omega = 0.5,
                           r = 1, alpha = 0.025, tar.power = 0.8, Test = 'CMH',
                           effect = 'OR', ss.method = 'standard', N.max = 160,
                           theta = seq(0.05, 0.95, by = 0.05))
tie
mx <- attr(tie, 'max')
```

The largest type I error rate of the re-estimation design with 20 patients per group and stratum is `r sprintf('%.5f', mx$TIE[1])`, at $(\theta_1, \theta_2) =$ (`r sprintf('%.3f', mx$theta.S1[1])`, `r sprintf('%.3f', mx$theta.S2[1])`), and no rate in the rectangle exceeds `r sprintf('%.5f', mx$bound[1])`. That of the fixed design is `r sprintf('%.5f', mx$TIE[2])`.

```{r tie-plot}
plot(tie)
```

`StratAlphaAdjBSSR()` lowers the nominal level until the certified largest rate does not exceed `alpha`.

```{r alpha-adj}
adj <- StratAlphaAdjBSSR(Delta.A = 2.5, N1 = c(20, 20), N2 = c(20, 20), omega = 0.5,
                         r = 1, alpha = 0.025, tar.power = 0.8, Test = 'CMH',
                         effect = 'OR', ss.method = 'standard', N.max = 160,
                         theta = seq(0.05, 0.95, by = 0.05))
adj
```

## Three or more strata

With three or more strata the number of interim outcomes grows as a product over the strata, and `StratPowerBSSR()` and `StratTypeIErrorBSSR()` estimate the rates of the re-estimation design by simulation, with the random numbers of R and a Monte Carlo standard error. The rates of the fixed design remain exact.

```{r three-strata}
set.seed(1)
q2 <- c(0.2, 0.35, 0.5)
q1 <- q2 * 2.5 / (1 - q2 + q2 * 2.5)
plan3 <- StratSampleSize(q1, q2, frac = c(0.3, 0.3, 0.4), alpha = 0.025,
                         tar.power = 0.8, Test = 'CMH', method = 'standard')
res3 <- StratPowerBSSR(p = (q1 + q2) / 2, Delta.A = 2.5, Delta.T = 2.5, N1 = plan3$N1,
                       N2 = plan3$N2, omega = 0.5, r = 1, alpha = 0.025, tar.power = 0.8,
                       Test = 'CMH', effect = 'OR', ss.method = 'standard',
                       N.max = 2 * plan3$N, nsim = 2e4)
res3[, c('power.BSSR', 'se.BSSR', 'power.TRAD', 'E.N')]
```

## References

Jung SH (2014). Stratified Fisher's exact test and its sample size calculation. *Biometrical Journal*, 56(1), 129-140.

Nam J (1992). Sample size determination for case-control studies and the comparison of stratified and unstratified analyses. *Biometrics*, 48(2), 389-395.

Woolson RF, Bean JA, Rojas PB (1986). Sample size for case-control studies using Cochran's statistic. *Biometrics*, 42(4), 927-932.
